patient.chief_complaint: Sudden onset left-sided weakness and inability to speak
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Jennings is a 72-year-old right-handed man with a history of atrial fibrillation (not on anticoagulation), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia who was brought to the emergency department by EMS after his wife found him slumped in his recliner at approximately 14:30 today. She reports that they had eaten lunch together at 12:15 and he was entirely at his baseline at that time, conversant and eating without difficulty with both hands. She went to run errands and returned home at 14:25, at which point she found him leaning to the right in his chair with his left arm hanging limply at his side. He appeared to be trying to speak but could only produce unintelligible sounds. She immediately called 911. EMS arrived at 14:38 and noted right gaze deviation, left facial droop, left-sided hemiplegia, and global aphasia. A prehospital stroke alert was activated. Finger-stick glucose in the field was 168 mg/dL. He was transported emergently to our comprehensive stroke center. On arrival at 15:02, the patient was in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response on the cardiac monitor. He appeared anxious and was making repetitive vocalizations but no recognizable words. There was no reported preceding headache, seizure activity, recent head trauma, or febrile illness. His wife confirms he has not been taking any blood thinners. She notes he has been generally well recently with no recent hospitalizations or illness. His last known well time is established at 12:15 today, approximately 2 hours and 47 minutes prior to ED arrival.

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast head CT MUST exclude intracranial hemorrhage before IV thrombolysis is considered (tPA decision modeled here through drug-interaction/contraindication check).
Glucose, INR/PTT, and platelet count must be reviewed before IV thrombolysis to exclude hypoglycemia mimic and coagulopathy contraindications.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Activate stroke code; assess thrombectomy eligibility for LVO on CTA
Administer IV tPA if within window and no contraindications
Restart anticoagulation post-stroke for AF (DOAC preferred unless valvular AF)
Engage shared decision-making to address future adherence
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not discharge on antiplatelet alone for AF-related cardioembolic stroke
Do not delay thrombectomy referral when LVO is documented
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
AF without anticoagulation has an annual stroke risk ~5% (higher with additional risk factors)
Proximal LMCA occlusion is a thrombectomy-eligible LVO up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 criteria
Bridging IV tPA + thrombectomy is the standard for eligible patients
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward - classic presentation with sudden onset right hemiparesis and aphasia, known AF not on anticoagulation, clear LVO on imaging
clinical_pearls: Time is brain: every minute of delayed reperfusion results in loss of approximately 1.9 million neurons
AF is the most common cause of cardioembolic stroke, and patients with AF-related stroke have higher recurrence rates without anticoagulation
The combination of IV tPA and mechanical thrombectomy (bridging therapy) is superior to IV tPA alone for LVO
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Classic cardioembolic LMCA stroke with known AF off anticoagulation, witness-confirmed onset; one dominant mechanism.

LATERALIZATION CONTRADICTION: imaging + ground_truth describe a LEFT MCA infarct (left M1/ICA-T occlusion) and the exam shows global aphasia (left/dominant hemisphere) — internally consistent. BUT the motor/sensory/gaze/face findings and HPI are all LEFT-sided body deficits (left hemiplegia, left facial droop, right gaze preference, left hemineglect, left extinction, tongue deviates left), which is the RIGHT-hemisphere pattern and the OPPOSITE of what a left MCA stroke produces (should be right-sided deficits). A left MCA stroke causing left-body deficits is not coherent. Needs human adjudication: either flip the lesion side to RIGHT MCA (but then global aphasia does not fit in a right-handed patient) or flip the body-side findings to RIGHT. Flagged, not auto-edited (touches clinical story across HPI + multiple exam fields).
